en: No matter what you're building with Bun,
chances are that your application or tool
needs some environment variables or uses
some environment variables. And turns out
Bun makes using such variables and loading
them into the program a breeze too. No extra
packages or dependencies are needed. It's
all built in. And to show this feature, I'm
back in a new project, which isn't that new.
It's that SQLite project I showed you in an
earlier lesson. Lecture, but now there is a
.env file in there, as you may have it in
many projects. And in that.env file, I
store my DB path to make that easily
configurable and also so that if I were to
deploy this application, I could set this
environment variable on the host I deploy it
to, to easily control where that database
file would be stored on that host where the
app may be deployed to. Now, this is of
course not Bun exclusive or specific, but in
the past, you
may have used extra packages for loading
that file. You also may have extra files
like.env.local to have different
environment variables locally than you may
have on the staging server or the production
server. So things like that is also
something you may have or want.
And when using Bun, those files are found
and loaded automatically. So if you have a
.env file or a.env.local file in your
project folder, Bun will find and load them
automatically
when you run bun run
and then run your program. If you don't want
to load those files for whatever reason, you
could add
--no-env-file
and then run your program. So that would
work.
And if you have specific files that aren't
picked up by Bun, you can run bun run
--env-file And you can add that flag
multiple times if you have multiple files
and then point at the file you wanna load.
But here I'm pointing at.env and this is
not needed because as mentioned, this file
will be found automatically. Still, you can
of course do it if you wanna be extra
explicit and clear about it.
Now in my program in dbts, I'm then using
values from that.env file. I'm getting my
DB_PATH and I do that with the same syntax
you may know from Node.js using process.env
and then the name of the environment
variable I'm interested in and that of
course in my case is the DB_PATH env var I'm
setting here.
Bun also offers alternative syntaxes you
could use. You could also load environment
variables through its bun.env
feature, its bun.env property. That is
simply an alternative to using process.env
or the more modern import.meta.env but all 3
approaches will yield the same result. They
give you that environment variable which I'm
then using here.
By the way, for SQLite, just as a side note,
if you don't set a value here, it will just
create an in-memory database by default. So
it won't crash if this environment variable
wouldn't be set or if it would be set to an
empty string or anything like that, but it
would create an in-memory database in that
case. But that is how you can easily load
and use environment variables with Bun.
